<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par69 />{{GHGterm|Yôdh}}, or, lastly, is altogether elided; (''b'') Verbs which (as in Arabic) originally began with {{GHGterm|Yôdh}} (called ''Verba cum Iod originario'', see § 70). A few verbs again (some with original {{GHGterm|Yôdh}}, and some with original {{GHGterm|Wāw}}) form a special class, which in certain forms assimilates the {{GHGterm|Wāw}} or ''Yâdh'' to the following consonant on the analogy of the ''Nûn'' in verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״ן}} (see § 71).

{{GHGmargin-letter|69|b}}
With regard to verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״ו}} (i.e. {{GHGheb|text=פ״י}} with original {{GHGterm|Wāw}}) it is to be noticed that—

'''1.''' In the ''imperfect, imperative'' and ''infinitive construct Qal'' there is a twofold inflexion, according as the {{GHGterm|Wāw}} is wholly rejected or only changed into {{GHGterm|Yôdh}}. The complete rejection (or ''elision'') takes place regularly in eight verbs (see h) in the following manner:

A. {{GHGterm|Imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יֵשֵׁב}}, {{GHGheb|text=יֵדַע}} with an unchangeable<ref>The ''e'' of the first syllable is really ''ê'', not tone-long ''ē'', since it is retained not merely before the tone, and in the counter-tone (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וְיֵדָֽעֵם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=14|verse=10}}), but also in {{GHGheb|text=אֵדָֽעֲךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=13.17}}. It is no objection to this view that the ''scriptio plena'' of this ''ê'' occurs (with the exception of {{GHGheb|text=יֵיקַר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=72|verse=14}}, elsewhere pointed {{GHGheb|text=יִיקַר}}) only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=1|verse=8}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=35|verse=9}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=138|verse=6}} the Masora prefers to point {{GHGheb|text=יְיֵדָע}}.—Of the various explanations of the ''ê'' the most satisfactory is that of Philippi ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xl. p. 653) that an original ''yălĭd'', for example (see above), became ''yilid'' by assimilation of the vowel of the first syllable to that of the second; this then became ''yêlēd'' instead of ''yēlēd'', in an attempt to raise the word again in this way (by writing ''ê'' instead of ''ē'') to a triliteral form.</ref> {{GHGterm|Ṣere}} in the first syllable and original ''ĭ'' in the second, which in the tone-syllable (according to {{GHGpar|27|c}}) becomes ''ē'' (thus {{GHGheb|text=יֵלֵד}}, {{GHGheb|text=יֵצֵא}}, {{GHGheb|text=יֵלֵךְ ;יֵרֵד}}, see x), or, under the influence of a guttural, with ''ă'' in the second ({{GHGheb|text=יֵדַע}}, {{GHGheb|text=יֵקַע}}, {{GHGheb|text=יֵחַד}}).

The tone-long ''ē'' of the second syllable is of course liable to be shortened or to become {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וַיֵּ֫שֶׁב}}, {{GHGheb|text=יֵֽשְׁבוּ}}, &c.; in the same way ''ă'' becomes {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} in such cases as {{GHGheb|text=יֵֽדְעוּ}}, &c., but is lengthened to {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} in {{GHGterm|pause}} ({{GHGheb|text=יֵדָ֫עוּ}}) and before suffixes ({{GHGheb|text=יֵֽדָעֵם}}).

B. {{GHGterm|Imperative}} {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁב}} with ''aphaeresis'' of the {{GHGterm|Wāw}} and with tone-long ''ē'', from ''ĭ'', as in the {{GHGterm|imperfect}}.

C. {{GHGterm|Infinitive}} {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בֶת}} from original ''šibh'', by addition of the feminine ending ({{GHGheb|text=ת}}) lengthened to a ''segholate'' form; as in verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״ן}} (cf. {{GHGpar|66|b}}) this lengthening affords a certain compensation for loss of the initial consonant.

{{GHGmargin-letter|69|c}}
Rem. Since the infinitives {{GHGheb|text=דֵּעָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֵדָה}} (see below, m) point to a ground-form ''diʿat, lidat'', we must, with Philippi ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xxxii. 42) and Barth (ibid. xli. 606), assign to {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בֶת}}, &c., the ground-form ''šibt'' (which, therefore, reappears in {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְתִּי}}, &c.); the apparent ground-form ''šabt'' rests upon the law that the ''ĭ'' of the stem-syllable is changed into ''a'' whenever the syllable becomes doubly closed by the addition of the vowelless feminine ending.<section end=par69 /><noinclude>
